title: Education as a Space Inbetween
author: Nicola Peacock
summary: In this deeply personal essay, Nicola Peacock reconstructs three moments across her life, being retrieved from a dropped-out A-level path by a teacher at sixteen, returning to university at twenty-four after eighteen months of clinical depression, and enrolling in a master's degree in her forties amid divorce and grief, to argue that education's most important function is often invisible to outcome-focused metrics. Rather than framing school and university primarily as sites of safety or credentialing, she develops a more specific claim: that education can temporarily 'carry' more of a person's cognitive and emotional load than they can carry alone, reducing not the complexity of a difficult life but what is actively being asked of the person within it. She illustrates this with the felt experience of being 'a student again,' a role in which the task is simply to learn rather than to organize the future or continually prove competence, and traces how each return to formal study, whether prompted by an intervening teacher or self-initiated during crisis, allowed her to inhabit the world differently for the duration of the structure it provided. The essay closes by reframing her own recurring return to education not as love of learning per se but as a repeated discovery that a present circumstance need not define a future boundary.
points: Peacock's central conceptual move reframes education's value beyond safety or outcomes, arguing it can function as an external structure that temporarily 'carries' cognitive and emotional load a person cannot carry alone, reducing what's being asked of them rather than the complexity of their life itself.

Her account of teachers at her working-class secondary school (assuming university was possible 'long before I believed it was') illustrates how expectation-setting by educators can operate as a distinct causal factor in life trajectory, independent of the safety function of school.

The essay explicitly separates 'being a student' as a temporary role from being a lifelong learner as an identity, arguing the specific relief comes from a bounded period where the task is simply to learn rather than to solve every problem.

She uses her own repeated return to formal education at three life stages (adolescence, post-depression at 24, post-divorce in her 40s) as evidence that this restorative function of education operates independent of career necessity, since none of the returns were purely instrumental.

Her closing reframe, that education's value lies in demonstrating 'their present situation need not become the boundary of their future,' offers educators a way to think about the non-measurable, identity-level stakes of the students they retrieve or fail to retrieve at critical moments.
quotes: My English teacher had come to ask why I had not returned to school. ... I remember the fear that settled almost instantly in the pit of my stomach. Not because I had been found... but because I knew the volatility of the man standing on the other side of the front door.

I have never questioned that my English teacher changed the course of my life. Had she not stood on that doorstep on a September evening, I suspect my life would have followed an entirely different trajectory.

Teachers expected me to think. They expected me to read beyond the set text, to wrestle with ideas, to argue a point and support it with evidence. They assumed that university was a possibility long before I believed it was.
Education did not reduce the complexity of my life. It temporarily reduced what was being asked of me within it.
My task was not to organise the future, solve every problem or continually prove my competence. My task was to learn.
At certain moments in a life, education can become an environment that temporarily carries more than the individual can. Not permanently and not as an escape from responsibility, but long enough.

I think I returned because, at several crucial moments, learning offered me a way of inhabiting the world differently. It allowed me, for a while, to step out of the role I had been carrying and into one where growth itself was enough.
